— Conflicting opinions and research outcomes

d1, d4, d5, and d6 report large meta-analyses concluding all studied antidepressants are more effective than placebo, while d2, d8, and d9 present analyses showing only minimal average differences versus placebo or no superiority for SSRIs/SNRIs. d7 and d10 argue that for certain subgroups or when compared to psychotherapy, drug–placebo differences are negligible.

The retrieved evidence presents two incompatible research narratives about antidepressant efficacy versus placebo. Large meta-analyses pooling hundreds of randomized controlled trials consistently report that all studied antidepressants are more effective than placebo in reducing depressive symptoms over acute treatment periods [d1,d4,d5,d6]. In contrast, participant-level FDA-submitted trial analyses and broader critiques find only minimal average differences between drug and placebo and suggest that benefit may be confined to a minority of patients or contexts [d2,d8,d9]. Subgroup analyses further indicate negligible drug–placebo differences among antidepressant-naive patients, complicating any blanket claim of superiority [d7,d10].

Given these mutually exclusive conclusions within the same scope and time window, the evidence supports the conflict label.

Antidepressants are more effective than placebo according to large meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials [d1,d4,d5,d6]. However, other analyses show only a small average advantage over placebo and question whether this translates into meaningful clinical benefit for most patients [d2,d8,d9]. Subgroup findings suggest little to no advantage for antidepressant-naive individuals [d7,d10].
